OP I know you asked about recognizing an abusive relationship, but it's also important to recognize that there are ways to reduce the chance of even being in one. This includes maintaining a strong support structure (parents, longtime friends, etc), high degree of emotional and mental resilience/independence, being self-confident and self-assured, practicing skepticism, and understanding societal structure enough to confidently know your own place in it. Most abusers are quite paranoid (due to combined inferiority/superiority complexes), and on the lookout for the above signs, so keep a strong facade however you can.

Abuse is basically a kind of con job being pulled in slow motion. It's less like a bank robbery, and more like slowly turning up the heat to boil frogs without them noticing and escaping the pan. You can understand how an abuser thinks. A lot of abusers have justified their own actions under banners like, "The rest of the world always takes advantage of me, so it's no problem if I take advantage of this one person", "Everything's meaningless anyway", "OP is such a badass that they don't really care if I hurt them", or "You're a bad person and my abuse is actually helping society by hurting you".

Know that there are some astounding abusers out there, so whatever you do, they can probably still get around all your instincts and abuse you. However these people are (luckily) pretty rare, and pick their targets with cares.

The common thread in every abuser's thought process is a lack of respect for the other person. They also like to forgo the normal development of trust in interpersonal relationships, preferring instead to get up close to you by focusing only on your vulnerabilities ("I can make you a better person") or only on your strengths ("Teach me how to be awesome").

Lastly OP, just a small request: most abusers have been pretty badly abused themselves in their lives, and instead of dealing with it in a productive and reasonable manner, have chosen to attack and ruin other people's lives. I believe that their initial abuse deserves some sympathy even if their actions are bad. However, please, if you've been abused, you can deal with it in productive, constructive, good ways without harming others. A lot of abused people later become abusers. A lot of people don't realize that phrases like "walking on eggshells, excessive preoccupation about upsetting others, etc" apply equally as well to abusers as well as to the abused. Most abusers are merely abused people who've chosen to mentally leapfrog their way into looking like the helpless victim even if they're the one doing the abusing. Don't be a victim. Be responsible for your life and avoid excuses like "I'm always the victim".

Finally, note that a lot of people have directly or indirectly dealt with abuse, so it's basically a part of living life. It's quite survivable, just don't overcommit in any relationship, and look before you leap. After you've dealt with abuse one or two times, you'll become a natural at recognizing and avoiding it.

If you've never been in a romantic relationship, and you're worried about abuse, there's a chance that you might also see some when there isn't any. It's important to note that with SOME factors, there's a grey area. For example (and I'll exaggerate a bit here) they say abuse is attempting to limit time spent with family and friends -- but if you haven't seen your SO in two weeks or so, but you've seen your friends a bunch, and your SO asks you to stay with them instead, that's not abuse. That sounds reasonable to me.

Abuse makes you feel tortured on the inside. Abuse makes you feel like you're putting in your best effort and nothing is coming out the way you've tried to make it. Sometimes, abusive relationships have nothing to do with the abuser choosing to be abusive (though... yes, there are clearly psychos who just enjoy the abusive act), abuse can manifest as simply staying in the wrong relationship, where your love languages don't match up and you cannot communicate and things are falling apart. You both may feel that you're doing your best, and you want to make it work, but it isn't, and you both end up abused because of it.

The most I can say to you in terms of not falling into an abusive trap is this: Your relationship should not feel like a roller coaster. It should feel more like sticking your hand out of a moving car window on the highway. A roller coaster will bring you amazing thrills, but also force you down to the lowest, most desperate of lows, terrifying you on the way. But making a hand airplane out of the window never scares you. It's never shocking. The ups and downs both feel pleasant enough, and you always feel like you're flying.

I think I can say that I'm in my first relationship right now that is not abusive in any way, and that's the only reason I feel I have been able to retroactively realize just how bad all my others were. You wouldn't believe how fantastic the communication is. No matter what I have to say, I know my partner will take it in stride and work with me to make our relationship work. They won't call me crazy, say it's irrational, expect me to change, or anything. They accept it, and we find a way to work accordingly. Sure, we have good and bad days, but even our worst days are still some of the best.
